uncited: It solves the problem of providing fragment shaders with precise start and end texture coordinates for volume traversal without complex CPU-side ray-box intersection calculations [S2, unofficial].
- **Inputs:** Camera projection matrix, model-view matrix, volume bounding box geometry (cube), and a boolean flag `m_bFront` to select front (entry) or back (exit) hit computation.
- **Outputs:** Two 2D textures (`TEXTURE_FRONT_HIT` and `TEXTURE_BACK_HIT`) storing the 3D world-space hit positions (or texture coordinates) for each pixel.
- **Hit Textures:** 2D textures of size `Width x Height` (screen resolution).
The vertex shader passes the vertex position and normal.
The geometry shader receives the triangle vertices, computes the ray-box intersection for the ray defined by the camera origin and the fragment's screen position, and outputs the hit position.
For each vertex, it computes the ray direction from the camera origin to the vertex.
It then performs a ray-box intersection test (using the slab method from [Ray-box intersection](776-ray-box-intersection.md)) to find the entry and exit points.
The hit position is written to the output.
- **Time Complexity:** O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the screen resolution, as each pixel requires a ray-box intersection computation in the geometry shader.
- **Memory Complexity:** O(W * H) for storing the hit textures, where W and H are the screen dimensions.
- **Measured Performance:** Not given in the sources.
Simple to implement using standard OpenGL features.
- **When to use:** When GPU-based ray-box intersection is desired and OpenGL geometry shaders are available.
- **When not to use:** When high precision is required (use 32-bit textures or CPU-side computation) or when geometry shaders are not supported.
It is used in the context of GPU-accelerated volume rendering to efficiently compute ray-box intersections for volume traversal.
